name: Sulbutiamine

lead: Sulbutiamine is a synthetic compound made of two thiamine (vitamin B1) units, designed to be fat-soluble so it enters the body and brain more readily. People take it for more energy, motivation and mental stamina, which supports staying consistent with training and routines.

Servier has marketed it in France since 1973 as Arcalion for asthenia. After absorption it is reduced to thiamine, and rodent and cell studies show it raises thiamine phosphate levels, including in brain tissue. Human data come from small studies, including an uncontrolled trial in multiple sclerosis fatigue.

paras: Taken as an oral supplement, typically in the morning, and used as an energy or mental-stamina aid. Many users take it only occasionally rather than every day because of tolerance.

Trials mostly report headache and stomach discomfort at high doses. Daily use can lead to tolerance and paradoxical drowsiness. Other reports include diarrhea, insomnia, constipation and vertigo. It is not FDA-approved as a drug and appears on a US Department of Defense prohibited supplement list.

angle.text: Sulbutiamine is taken for less fatigue and more energy and motivation, which helps people keep up their training and routines. It is prescribed for asthenia in France; human data are sparse and no appearance outcome has been studied.

lead: Sulbutiamine (isobutyrylthiamine disulfide) is a synthetic, lipophilic derivative of thiamine in which two thiamine molecules are linked by a disulfide bridge.[1] Servier marketed it in France from 1973 as Arcalion, and it is prescribed there for asthenia.[1]
It is also sold as a dietary supplement, and some users take it as a nootropic.[1] Evidence is limited, and a 1980s French review found the data did not support use in fatigue.[1]

paras: It is a fat-soluble disulfide that is reduced to thiamine after absorption.[1] In neuroblastoma cells it entered far faster than thiamine and was rapidly converted to free thiamine.[2] Injection in rats raised thiamine triphosphate in tissues.[3] Studies in mice reported improved long-term memory formation with a possible cholinergic mediation.[4] Grokipedia describes Tanabe Pharmaceutical development in Japan in the mid-1960s.[5]

Wikipedia reports that trials explored chronic fatigue syndrome, that a 2017 uncontrolled trial reported reduced fatigue in people with multiple sclerosis, and that whether it helps with drowsiness is unclear.[1] A registered trial is studying nocturnal enuresis in children.[6] No randomized trial of sulbutiamine for appearance has been identified.

Headache and gastrointestinal discomfort at high doses are most reported, with tolerance and paradoxical drowsiness described with daily use; diarrhea, insomnia, constipation and vertigo have also been noted.[1]
Laboratory work has examined protection of retinal ganglion cells[7] and anticancer and diabetic nephropathy models in rodents.[8]

timeline.event: Servier markets sulbutiamine in France as Arcalion.[1]
100 mg tablets discontinued in favor of 200 mg.[1]
